titulo.en: I had, I was, I could, I came

objetivo.en: Tell what happened in the past, like your trip from Chicago to Quito, with the irregular preterites of tener, estar, poder, poner, venir, querer, decir and traer.

nota.en: Plural: los aviones (the accent mark disappears).
In Chicago, winter means a lot of snow.
Snow does not fall in the city of Quito.
Plural: las mamás, with the accent. Madre is the more formal word.
Tener miedo = to be afraid: tuve miedo = I was scared.
Latin America says boleto; Spain says billete.

explicacion.en: These irregular preterites have no accent mark: tuve, estuve, pude, puse, vine. The accent belongs only to regular verbs like hablé.
After a j in the stem, the ending is -eron, not -ieron: dijeron, trajeron.
The él/ella form of these verbs ends in -o, with no i and no accent: quiso, tuvo, pudo, vino.

titulo.en: Eight verbs with a new stem in the preterite

texto.en: You already know regular preterites such as hablé and comí, and also fui and hice. Eight very common verbs change their stem in the preterite: tener → tuv-, estar → estuv-, poder → pud-, poner → pus-, venir → vin-, querer → quis-, decir → dij- and traer → traj-. They all use the same endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron. Unlike regular preterites, these endings never carry an accent mark: tuve, tuvo, vine, vino. With dij- and traj- the ustedes/ellos form ends in -eron, not -ieron: dijeron, trajeron. Spanish v and b sound the same, so tuve, estuve and vine are all pronounced with a b sound (a soft one between vowels, as in tuve and estuve). A useful meaning to remember: tuve miedo means “I was scared”, and no pude means “I couldn’t (I tried, and it didn’t work)”.

titulo.en: Time words for a finished past

texto.en: Use these irregular preterites for things that happened and are over, usually with a time word such as ayer (yesterday), anoche (last night), el año pasado (last year) or en septiembre (in September). The time word can go at the start or the end of the sentence: Ayer tuve mucho trabajo. / Tuve mucho trabajo ayer.

titulo.en: He asked for, he slept, he preferred

objetivo.en: Tell what other people asked for, preferred and slept during a vacation, using the -ir verbs that change in the preterite.

nota.en: In Spain people say el bañador; in Ecuador, el traje de baño.
Raw or lightly cooked seafood in lime juice; a classic on the Ecuadorian coast.
For a woman: la mesera.
Pescado is fish you eat; pez is the live animal.
What you ask for at a restaurant.
In Ecuador: bloqueador solar, or just bloqueador.

explicacion.en: In the preterite, -ir verbs change the e to i in the él/ella form: prefirió, not preferió. The stress falls on the last syllable.
Dormir changes o to u in the ellos form of the preterite: durmieron.
Servir changes e to i in the él/ella form: sirvió, sirvieron.

titulo.en: -ir verbs that change in the third person

texto.en: Many -ir verbs change their stem in the present: pido, sirvo, prefiero, duermo. In the preterite they change too, but only in two forms: él/ella/usted and ustedes/ellos/ellas. The vowel e becomes i (pedir → pidió, pidieron; servir → sirvió; repetir → repitió; seguir → siguió; preferir → prefirió) and the vowel o becomes u (dormir → durmió, durmieron). The forms for yo, tú and nosotros do not change: pedí, pediste, pedimos; dormí, dormiste, dormimos. Be careful with preferir: it is prefirió and prefirieron, never preferió. Verbs in -ar and -er do not change their stem in the preterite.

titulo.en: Present or preterite?

texto.en: Compare a habit with a single event: Mi papá siempre pide pescado (he always asks for fish; present) but Ayer pidió pollo (yesterday he asked for chicken; preterite). Both forms start with the same letters, so listen to the ending: pide has the stress on the first syllable, and pidió has it on the last one.

titulo.en: Present and preterite side by side

texto.en: The present describes a habit; the preterite, something finished. Tap each form to hear it.

texto.en: Preferir changes e to i; dormir changes o to u. Tap each form to hear it.

titulo.en: I looked for, I arrived, I started, I read

objetivo.en: Spell the preterite of verbs in -car, -gar, -zar and of leer correctly to tell, in a message, what you did yesterday.

nota.en: Plural: las postales.
Buscar already includes the idea of “for”: say busqué la oficina, with no extra word.
Same meaning as empezar.

explicacion.en: A g followed by e would sound like a strong h. To keep the hard g sound in yo, write gu: llegué.
Verbs in -gar add u in the yo form of the preterite: pagué, jugué, llegué.
Spanish almost never writes z before e or i, so verbs in -zar change z to c in the yo form: empecé, almorcé.
An i between two vowels becomes y in the third-person forms of leer: leyó, leyeron.

titulo.en: Spelling changes in the yo form

texto.en: Verbs ending in -car, -gar and -zar change their spelling in the yo form of the preterite, so that the sound stays the same. Before e, the letter c would sound like s and g like a strong h, so Spanish writes qu (a k sound) and gu (a hard g sound; the u is silent): buscar → busqué (boos-KEH), llegar → llegué (yeh-GEH), pagar → pagué. And since z is almost never written before e, verbs in -zar change z to c: empezar → empecé, almorzar → almorcé. Only yo changes. All the other forms are regular: buscaste, buscó, buscamos, buscaron. Verbs such as guardar and copiar do not need any change: guardé, copié.

titulo.en: Leer: i becomes y

texto.en: Leer follows its own spelling rule. An i between two vowels turns into y in the third-person forms: leyó, leyeron. In the other forms the i stays, with an accent mark that tells you to pronounce the two vowels separately: leí, leíste, leímos. Watch the difference between leí (I read) and leyó (he/she read).

objetivo.en: Tell a special day in order, like your arrival in Quito, with primero, luego, después, más tarde and al final.

nota.en: As an adverb it never changes: primero, not primera.
Después and luego mean the same here; you can use either one.

traduccion.en: in the end, at the end

nota.en: Not “en el final”: Spanish says al final.

explicacion.en: After a time marker, conjugate the verb in the preterite: primero llegué, not the infinitive.

titulo.en: Telling a day in order

texto.en: To tell what happened in order, use time markers and the preterite. Primero means “first”. Luego and después both mean “then” or “afterwards”. Más tarde means “later”, and al final means “in the end”. Usually the marker opens the sentence: Primero llegué al aeropuerto. Luego tomé un taxi. Al final dormí. Primero can also go after the verb, but then it often means “ahead of the others”: Llegué primero a casa (I got home first, before the others).

titulo.en: When I was a girl…

objetivo.en: Describe how things used to be, like your childhood, your house and your grandfather, and what you used to do.

nota.en: For a boy: el niño. De niña = as a girl; de niño = as a boy.
Plural: los jardines (the accent mark disappears).
For an aunt: la tía.
The school for children and teenagers.
Jugar is used for games and sports: jugar fútbol or jugar al fútbol.
No accent mark here. With an accent, ¿cuándo? is the question “when?”.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Mi abuelo ía a mi casa los domingos.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Mi abuelo iba a mi casa los domingos.

explicacion.en: Ir does not use the -ía ending. It is one of the three irregular verbs: iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, iban.
In -ar verbs, the nosotros form of the imperfect carries an accent mark on the first a: hablábamos, jugábamos.
English says “I was living”, but the Spanish imperfect is a single word: vivía. You don’t need ser or estar before it.

titulo.en: The imperfect: how things were

texto.en: The imperfect describes the background of the past: how people, places and things were (Mi casa era pequeña) and what you used to do again and again (Los domingos veíamos fútbol). In English it is often “used to” or “was/were”. It is the tense for telling about your childhood: Cuando era niña, vivía en Chicago. It does not say when something began or ended, only what it was like. The three irregular verbs are ser, ir and ver; every other verb follows the pattern.

titulo.en: Endings of the imperfect

texto.en: Verbs in -ar take -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -aban: hablaba, jugaba. Verbs in -er and -ir take -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían: comía, vivía, tenía. There are no stem changes. Yo and él/ella have the same form (yo vivía, ella vivía), so use the pronoun or the context when it is not clear who you mean. In the nosotros form of -ar verbs, the accent mark goes on the first a: hablábamos.

titulo.en: Imperfect of -ar verbs: hablar, jugar

texto.en: Same endings for every -ar verb. Tap each form to hear it.

titulo.en: Imperfect of -er and -ir verbs: comer, vivir, tener

texto.en: Same endings for -er and -ir verbs. Tap each form to hear it.

titulo.en: The three irregular verbs: ser, ir, ver

texto.en: Learn these three by heart. Tap each form to hear it.

contexto.en: One afternoon in the Andrades’ kitchen, Señora Rosa asks Emma about her life as a girl. Emma uses usted with her; Rosa uses tú.

dialogo.texto: Emma, ¿cómo era tu vida de niña?

traduccion.en: Emma, what was your life like as a girl?

dialogo.texto: Vivía en Chicago con mis padres, señora Rosa.

traduccion.en: I lived in Chicago with my parents, Mrs. Rosa.

dialogo.texto: ¿Y cómo era tu casa?

traduccion.en: And what was your house like?

dialogo.texto: Era pequeña, pero tenía un jardín muy bonito.

traduccion.en: It was small, but it had a very pretty garden.

dialogo.texto: ¿Y tu abuelo?
Mi abuelo era de Guadalajara. Los domingos iba a mi casa y veíamos fútbol.

traduccion.en: My grandfather was from Guadalajara. On Sundays he used to come to my house and we used to watch soccer.

dialogo.texto: ¿Hablaban español en casa?

traduccion.en: Did you speak Spanish at home?

dialogo.texto: No, hablábamos solo inglés.
Ahora hablas mucho español con nosotros. ¡Qué bien!

traduccion.en: Now you speak a lot of Spanish with us. How great!

feedback.en: Emma says: “Hablábamos solo inglés.”
